title: Être and avoir
topic: être and avoir in the present; subject pronouns; definite and indefinite articles; gender and plural of nouns
why: This first lesson lays the foundations: être and avoir, the subject pronouns, tu or vous, and the articles that carry the gender of every noun. With them you can already say who you are, where you are, how old you are and what you have.

Être and avoir: the two key verbs

Like English, French builds a huge number of sentences on two verbs: être (to be) and avoir (to have). Both are irregular, so learn them by heart, as a little chant: they are the foundation of everything that follows.

être (to be)avoir (to have)
je / j'je suisj'ai
tutu estu as
il, elle, onil estil a
nousnous sommesnous avons
vousvous êtesvous avez
ils, ellesils sontils ont

The subject pronouns

  • je becomes j' before a vowel: always j'ai, never “je ai”. This is called elision.
  • il and elle mean “he” and “she”, but also “it”: a thing is il or elle depending on its gender.
  • on means “we” in everyday speech, with the verb of il: on est à Paris = nous sommes à Paris.
  • ils is for men or a mixed group; elles only for a group of women.

Tu or vous?

English has one “you”, French has two. Use tu with a friend, your family or a child. Use vous with a stranger, in a shop, with your boss… and whenever you speak to several people.

Tu es anglais ?Are you English? (to a friend)
Vous êtes anglais ?Are you English? (formal, or to several people)

Listen to the plural: ils‿ont (they have) has a buzzing “z” sound, ils sont (they are) a hissing “s”. Same for nous‿avons and vous‿êtes: the final s of the pronoun is linked to the vowel with a “z”.

Le, la, les; un, une, des

In French, every noun has a gender: masculine or feminine. Not only people, but also objects and ideas: le livre (the book) is masculine, la clé (the key) is feminine. There is no real logic, so always learn a noun with its article, as one block: not “livre” but le livre, un livre.

thea / some
masculinele livreun livre
femininela voitureune voiture
before a vowel or silent hl'école, l'amiune école, un ami
plural (both genders)les livresdes livres

Before a vowel, le and la both become l', so the article no longer shows the gender: that's why dictionaries write l'école (f.) or l'ami (m.).

A silent plural

The plural usually adds an -s, but this -s is not pronounced: le livre and les livres sound exactly the same, except for the article (“luh” / “lay”). In French, you hear the plural on the little word in front, not on the noun.

J'ai des livres et des stylos.I have books and pens.
Les clés sont à l'école.The keys are at school.

des is the plural of un / une. English often uses no word at all (“I have books”), but French needs one: j'ai des livres, never “j'ai livres”.

", "

Nationality, age and a few jobs

Nationalities change with the person: add an -e for a woman. Two differences with English: they take no capital letter after être (je suis anglais), and the feminine changes the sound.

masculinefeminineEnglish
françaisfrançaiseFrench
anglaisanglaiseEnglish
américainaméricaineAmerican
canadiencanadienneCanadian
irlandaisirlandaiseIrish

In the masculine, the final consonant is silent: anglais ends on the vowel. With the -e of the feminine, the s is heard as a “z”: anglaise. In the plural, add -s: ils sont américains, elles sont canadiennes (no change for français, which already ends in -s).

Je suis anglaise et Paul est irlandais.I'm English (a woman speaking) and Paul is Irish.

For your studies or your job, French uses no article after être: je suis étudiant (I'm a student), elle est médecin. Lesson 5 comes back to this.

Age: with avoir, never être

In French, you have your years: j'ai trente ans, literally “I have thirty years”. English speakers often say “je suis trente”: it means nothing in French. And ans (years) is never left out. Take vingt (20), trente (30) and quarante (40) as they are for now: numbers come in unit 2.

Tu as vingt ans ? — Non, j'ai trente ans !Are you twenty? — No, I'm thirty!

A question can be just a statement with a rising voice: Tu as un stylo ? In writing, French puts a space before ? and !.
